reading: The speaker asks when it will be possible to wander without distinctions of cāti. The negative இல்லாமல் modifies the wandering, and the first line invokes the authority of a teaching attributed to Ātikapilar.
alternative: The wish may concern how the speaker moves among social groups, or a state of freedom from classification itself.
limit: The question names no particular group and gives no account of the cited teaching.

reading: The speaker first desires a boon of nonbirth, then raises the possibility of medicine against dying if born. Across the last two lines the speaker addresses the mind, urging it to remember the Tillai lord’s lotus feet and calling that remembrance good medicine for it.
alternative: The closing medicine can be heard as the answer to the earlier puzzle or as a change of focus from bodily death to devotional constancy.
limit: The verse leaves the relation between nonbirth and deathlessness open and identifies no material remedy.

reading: Three repetitions of the condition “if the mind is upright” govern வேண்டா, which removes the need for mantra recitation and two acts involving breath. The last line shifts to an affirmative statement that the mantra itself becomes right.
alternative: செம்மை can stress moral rectitude or a mind brought into proper order. The latter broadens the relation to the practices named.
limit: The agent of practice is implicit. The distinction intended between வாயு and வாசி is underdetermined.

reading: Addressing the woman of wisdom, the speaker locates the guru and the cutting away of mental crookedness within. The final how-question challenges the prospect of applying puṭam while ignorant of what happens to the poruḷ.
alternative: The language can evoke the firing of a substance or use that transformation as a figure for inward work.
limit: The segmentation of பொருளிறப்பதறியாமற் and the referent of பொருள் are uncertain. The rhetorical question gives no procedure.

reading: The speaker asks when bliss will be attained. A sequence involving pride and the five senses leads to the paradox of sleeping without sleeping. The negative participle qualifies the immediately repeated positive verb.
alternative: The paradox may suggest wakeful stillness or withdrawal from sensory activity.
limit: No named state of consciousness or exact bodily practice appears. The division of the opening participles is less certain than the closing question.

reading: The concessive opening allows an object to be of whatever character. The closing nominal clause defines discernment as seeing that object’s true substance or meaning. The knower is generic.
alternative: மெய்ப்பொருள் can emphasize what a thing actually is, or the truth of a matter presented for consideration.
limit: The couplet leaves the object and the means of inquiry unspecified.

reading: The verse sets a pot with nine oozing openings against an admiring description of a broad-shouldered, bangled woman. The fool voices the praise while the outer dark skin governs what the eye perceives. The speaker uses the discrepancy to rebuke fascination.
alternative: The rebuke can fall chiefly on the admirer’s misperception or on desire for a body whose outer covering conceals its contents.
limit: The nine openings belong to the bodily image. The stanza does not enumerate them, and the woman’s own voice is absent.

reading: The first-person speaker recalls once holding the body in contempt and then finding an abiding reality within. The exalted one has taken up residence there as in a temple, which grounds the speaker’s present care for the body.
alternative: உறுபொருள் can emphasize the reality encountered or the value now recognized in the body.
limit: The speaker gives no regimen and does not name the indwelling one beyond the epithet.

reading: A speaker referring to a precious girl as mine petitions the addressed lord to embrace her so that she will not languish. The instrumental endings accumulate surrounding causes of distress, and the shining spear vocative identifies the divine addressee.
alternative: The petitioner can be heard as a maternal figure or another intimate advocate for the girl. The embrace carries both courtship and devotional force.
limit: Compressed compounds and word breaks limit certainty about individual sensory images and the petitioner’s precise kinship.

reading: The speaker points to “this young girl” and asks the spear-bearing lord to say “fear not,” so that she may escape suffering and wasting. The split அஞ்ச / லெனவேணும் embeds the requested reassurance in the petition. Moon and sea enter as causes of distress.
alternative: A separate advocate may speak for the girl, or a devotional speaker may dramatize their own longing in the third person.
limit: The speaker’s relation to the girl is unstated. The moon’s venom imagery gives no independent basis for a poisoning narrative.
